title: 🎙️ Repair Culture & Practical Tech
description: Today is about things you can fix, keep running, and pass on — repair culture, right-to-repair wins and setbacks, gear that outlives its manufacturer's support window, and the maker ethos of building to last rather than building to replace. We're interested in tools, devices, and projects where longevity, repairability, and self-sufficiency intersect, especially in rural and off-grid contexts where you can't just run to a repair shop. - Daily themed article selection for podcast generation

_podcast.theme_scoring_prompt:
Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Repair Culture & Practical Tech' — the right to repair movement, gear that outlasts its manufacturer, DIY fixes, and tools built for longevity.

OUT OF SCOPE — score 0-9: geopolitical conflict; natural disasters without an engineering or preparedness angle; wildlife and conservation; working-lands policy; Indigenous governance; science discoveries with no DIY or hardware relevance; financial market news.

CALIBRATION — apply this ladder to everything else. Hands-on hardware journalism counts fully even without an explicit right-to-repair hook.
- 80-100: Directly about repairability — right-to-repair legislation wins and losses, iFixit-style teardowns scoring repairability, gear designed for user serviceability, products outliving manufacturer support and how owners keep them running, permacomputing, vintage hardware still in active use, open-source hardware, Rossmann-style repair advocacy, 3D-printed replacement parts, battery replacement guides, rural and off-grid repair self-sufficiency.
- 55-79: Hands-on maker and DIY content — builds, modifications, hardware hacks, workshop projects, practical electronics guides with real technical depth, 3D printing hardware and filament, off-grid and solar gear, home lab hardware, tools and workshop equipment, battery and power tech. Most genuine hands-on hardware journalism belongs HERE, not below.
- 30-54: Gadget and device reviews with some technical substance; consumer electronics touching software longevity or ecosystem lock-in; hardware whose selling point is open firmware or modular design.
- 10-29: Surface-level product announcements, gadget speculation, leaked specs, general tech news with no hardware or repair angle.

ANCHORS: 'Framework Laptop 16 teardown: a 9/10 repairability score' → 98. 'Oregon's right-to-repair law takes effect' → 92. 'Building a solar-powered Raspberry Pi weather station' → 68. 'Samsung teases thinner bezels on next Galaxy' → 15.

Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

items.title: [Fast Company] Architectural models finally come to the browser
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

When the collaborative design software company Figma launched its public beta in 2016, its browser-based web and interface design tools were a quick hit, putting the startup head to head with the dominant design software company of the day, Adobe. The premise and the interface were so simple, Figma soon became a go-to tool for designers.

The building design software startup Motif wants to do the same thing for architectural models. Through its platform, architects and builders across a project team can design and visualize buildings, and then collaboratively review and augment their designs, all online.

Motif Design is a newly launched platform that is seeking to take on the established software tools of the architecture, engineering, and construction industries by making them more user-friendly and collaborative. The cofounder and CEO, Amar Hanspal, says the software that these industries rely on has for too long been overly complex and frustratingly difficult to use. Motif Design, he says, offers a new way, making it possible for even highly complex building models to be worked on simultaneously in real time by different teams.

“By making it browser based, we are making it very accessible. One of the challenges of the old stack has been that it’s very difficult to use, it’s inaccessible, stuff runs on only PCs,” he says.

Most modeling currently happens within the walled realm of software tools, where updates by one user have to be saved before others can make their own changes, individual files constantly being checked out and then remerged back in. Motif is taking the model-building tasks that are the core of architectural practice and allowing them to happen smoothly online, across the many teams that use them, running on a live database capable of recording every change to a model as it happens. “Just like Figma did with the design stack,” Hanspal says.

Motif Design complements Motif Review, a browser-based collaborative workspace launched in 2025, which designers can use to present, visualize, mark up, and gather feedback on models in real time. Motif Design now allows users to build those complex models from scratch, all within the shareable, accessible space of a web browser. “That is hard to do because buildings have an enormous amount of data and browsers have memory limitations,” Hanspal says. “Only recently could a browser run the math fast enough for someone to work in the model rather than just look at it.”

Hanspal understands the challenge of dealing with big architectural models. He’s a former co-CEO and chief product officer at Autodesk, the $7 billion company behind industry standard software like AutoCAD and Revit. Before leaving Autodesk in 2016, he spent two decades helping the architecture, engineering, and construction industries streamline their work with building information modeling (BIM), an approach that relies on massive 3D models of building projects that can be accessed by the many teams involved in turning the design to reality.

By the turn of the century, BIM had pushed the industries irreversibly past the days of hand drawings and paper documents. “It combined geometry with the database,” Hanspal says. “So not only did things look real, but . . . also, you could query the system and say, how many doors in the building, how many windows in the building, and you could derive all that knowledge. Now it’s been 27 years since we did that last innovation.”

The architecture and building industries are more than ready for something new, Hanspal argues. “Their practices evolved faster than their tools,” he says.

Motif isn’t the only company creating browser-based building modeling tools. Arcol and Snaptrude are two other startups with similar software, and more established products like SketchUp also offer browser-based modeling. But given Hanspal’s experience at Autodesk, Motif Design is built on a deep foundation of knowledge about the complexities and inefficiencies of advanced design software.

Artificial intelligence has opened up more opportunities for tools like Motif’s. Hanspal says a key part of Motif Design is its agent-native approach, baking in the ability to train and use AI agents to automate mundane design tasks with a high level of confidence. “In the practice of design, there’s a lot of boring stuff people have to do,” he says, from checking building codes to ensuring the square footage is correct to counting doors. “That’s the stuff that sucks the soul out of you.”

Hanspal says Motif is now being used by many of the “signature names” in architecture, including firms in the U.S., the U.K., and across the Nordics. For now, the platform is optimized for the most typical building types, from offices to retail to housing to schools. Hanspal argues designing large-scale projects isn’t the power of the platform. The point, he says, is to finally make it easier for building models to live, and evolve, online. “People could start with a blank screen and build the entire building in our product,” he says.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Common dry-cleaning chemical linked to triple the risk of liver scarring
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

A chemical commonly used in dry cleaning and found in some household products may be an overlooked threat to liver health. Researchers found that people with detectable levels of tetrachloroethylene (PCE) in their blood were three times more likely to have significant liver fibrosis, a dangerous buildup of scar tissue that can eventually lead to liver failure or cancer. The risk climbed sharply as PCE levels increased, even after accounting for factors such as age, sex, race, education, alcohol use, and metabolic conditions.

items.title: [Kagi Small Web] Which local LLM should you run?
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

whichllm is a useful Python CLI utility that autodetects your GPU/CPU/RAM and pulls benchmarks from Hugging Face to rank the local LLMs you can run on your system, based on a mix of benchmarks and projected token speeds on your machine.

I have a modest but respectable 16 GB of NVIDIA VRAM at my disposal, so unsurprisingly the top models it suggests for my hardware are in the Qwen 3 and Phi 4 families, as well as the always excellent gpt-oss-20b from OpenAI. These suggestions basically match my own experiments.

The top suggestion is Qwen3.6-27B, but the tool is basing it on stale benchmarks from May 2026 (I got a rate limiting error when it tried to pull the live benchmarks—I guess a lot of people are clamoring to test local LLMs).

If the tool was using live benchmarks, I believe it would almost certainly put Qwen3.8-27B at the very top, the model released a few weeks ago to rave reviews.

I was also curious which models it would recommend if I was running on CPU only. Surprisingly, the top suggestion was gpt-oss-20b, with a warning that all of the top contenders would run very slowly and that token speed estimates were uncertain.

items.title: [Fast Company] Nearly 200 Amazon workers called this pregnancy rights hotline in 2026. Now there’s a lawsuit
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Amazon is once again under fire for its work policies, this time with a new class action lawsuit filed against the retail giant on Tuesday that alleges the company has failed to make basic workplace accommodations for its pregnant employees.

The lawsuit, filed in a Brooklyn federal court, alleges that the Seattle-based company has engaged in a systematic and company-wide failure to accommodate pregnant workers and deliberately retaliated against them. The four named plaintiffs, all of whom were formerly employed at Amazon warehouses in New York, detail instances in which they claim they were denied work accommodations and subsequently disciplined or terminated, or faced retaliation during their pregnancies. 

The Pregnant Workers Fairness Act, which was signed into law by President Joe Biden in 2022 and went into effect in 2023, is key to this proposed nationwide class action lawsuit. That legislation requires employers to provide “reasonable accommodations” for qualified employees affected by pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions.

The new lawsuit alleges that Amazon’s policies violated the law in two ways—by requiring a pregnant worker to provide a doctor’s note before the company will provide even basic accommodations and by failing to account for legally protected pregnancy-related breaks. The plaintiffs are represented by Emery Celli Brinckerhoff Abady Ward & Maazel LLP, a civil rights law firm, and A Better Balance, a nonprofit advocacy organization, both of which have previously been involved in legislation against the retail giant.

“As our lawsuit details, Amazon regularly violates the law. Under its policies, pregnant workers are not protected, and they face retaliation for exercising their rights,” Debbie Greenberger, a partner at Emery Celli Brinckerhoff Abady Ward & Maazel LLP, said in a statement. “Too often, pregnant women working at Amazon warehouses have to risk their health or their pregnancy just to do their jobs.”   

An Amazon spokesperson told Fast Company the company conducted “thorough” internal reviews of each of the cases referenced in the lawsuit and noted that some of the details laid out in the suit contain inaccuracies and omit important details, but didn’t provide specifics. The company also noted that in the past year, 99.9% of pregnancy accommodation requests have been approved.

“Ensuring the health and well-being of our employees is one of our greatest responsibilities, and we strive to provide a safe and supportive environment for everyone, which includes supporting tens of thousands of employees with pregnancy accommodations each year,” Kelly Nantel, an Amazon spokesperson, said in a statement to Fast Company.

AMAZON’S POLICIES UNDER SCRUTINY

Amazon states on its website that it has a mission to be “Earth’s most customer-centric company, best employer, and safest place to work.” But a long list of lawsuits and other complaints over the years have contested the latter two points, in particular. 

There are currently dozens of open cases against the company with the National Labor Relations Board and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) for a broad range of alleged violations against workers. And the new lawsuit is hardly the first time that its treatment of pregnant workers has come under scrutiny.

In October 2025, New Jersey filed a civil rights lawsuit against Amazon, alleging it systematically violated state civil rights and pregnancy protection laws across its fulfillment centers, while New York made a similar complaint in 2022 that the company was engaging in discrimination against pregnant workers by denying them reasonable accommodations.

Earlier this year, the EEOC determined that Amazon had violated both the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act and the Americans With Disabilities Act. In February, the commission determined that the company had discriminated against Jennifer Hatch, one of the plaintiffs in the class action lawsuit, by failing to provide her with pregnancy-related accommodations. 

That same determination noted there was “reasonable cause” to believe the company had likewise discriminated against “a nationwide class of female warehouse associates” since 2023. The three other plaintiffs in the lawsuit similarly filed complaints against Amazon with the EEOC.

A BIGGER THREAT

As the new lawsuit notes, the four plaintiffs are likely indicative of a bigger problem with how Amazon treats its pregnant workforce. The suit seeks reforms of Amazon’s policies on behalf of the plaintiffs and a class of “similarly situated workers,” as well as compensation for past and ongoing violations of the law. 

The number of affected workers will likely go up as word spreads about the possible class action lawsuit, and the filing notes that A Better Place fielded calls from “dozens” of pregnant Amazon employees in 2025 who said the company had denied them basic accommodations. So far this year, nearly 200 Amazon workers have called the organization’s free helpline, its president Inimai Chettiar told USA Today. 

While Amazon may be the focus of this lawsuit, it is not an isolated incident and speaks to what’s at stake if critical protections for pregnant workers are rolled back, according to Chettiar.

“It actually sits inside a larger pattern of policy and rhetoric aimed at narrowing women’s roles and pushing them out of the workforce and back into a domestic role,” she told USA Today.

items.title: [Fast Company] Social media companies are using AI and face scans to spot more kids on their platforms
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Of the child safety measures agreed to in Meta’s landmark legal settlement, no category contains more detailed requirements than its commitments on age assurance—and for good reason. No matter how well the protections work, they are of little use if Meta can’t tell which users are kids.

Determining which accounts belong to children is also the linchpin of child safety measures that other companies, including Google, TikTok, and Roblox, are ramping up as public and regulatory sentiment turns against them in the U.S. and other countries.

The Meta settlement—with protections the company says could become industry standards—will give the social media giant a year to refine its approach. But the options are limited, and improving age verification technology presents steep challenges, including navigating privacy implications not just for children but for adults who could have to prove they are over 18.

The $18 billion settlement resolves claims from state attorneys general that it hurt children’s mental health by deliberately designing its Instagram and Facebook platforms in ways that hooked young people’s attention. The agreement announced last week with the Menlo Park, California, company involves 48 states plus the District of Columbia and U.S. territories.

Tech companies lean on AI for estimating ages

In the offline world, people use government-issued IDs to prove they are over 18 or 21, whether they want to get into a club or buy cigarettes. While this technically works online too, many people are not comfortable giving a Big Tech company like Meta or Google access to their driver’s license or passport.

Meta accepts IDs to check ages, and promises to delete them within 30 days. Beyond IDs, though, a growing number of tech companies are using artificial intelligence to try to determine users’ ages. This is not true age verification. While AI can estimate a person’s age, often accurately, it can’t verify a person’s birth date.

Last year, Google began using an age-assurance system for YouTube that relies on AI to differentiate between adults and minors based on their watch histories. Meta does the same.

AI age checks use clues to determine how old someone is. On Instagram, this includes “contextual clues” such as posts about birthday celebrations or school, and things like which posts people like, comment on, or linger on, who their friends are, as well as the times of day they log in. For instance, someone who is offline during school hours would likely be school-aged.

In a blog post last year, Meta said its AI also looks at photos people post for visual cues, including “height or bone structure, to estimate someone’s general age; it does not identify the specific person in the image.”

“By combining these visual insights with our analysis of text and interactions, we can significantly increase the number of underage accounts we identify and remove,” the company added.

Under the settlement, Meta agreed to strengthen its age-checking technology using its own tools, as well as third-party ones, with regular outside audits on how well it is working. The agreement also includes specific goals around false positive rates—that is, minors who are identified as over 18. And if a user is identified as under 13 and kicked off one of its platforms, Meta will check the ages of their friends, too.

Face scans count as age assurance on some sites

Identity verification companies like Yoti and Persona, which work with tech companies like Meta and Roblox, use video selfies people upload to estimate their ages.

The gaming site Roblox, which, unlike social media platforms, allows kids under 13 to sign up, requires players to take a video selfie to estimate their age. Roblox says the videos are deleted after the age check is processed. Users are not required to submit a face scan to use the platform, only if they want to chat with other users.

Some users have reported inaccuracies, and some experts have expressed caution about the reliability of facial age estimation tools, especially for women or certain racial or ethnic groups. But Matt Kaufman, chief safety officer at Roblox, said last year that for people between about 5 and 25, the system can accurately estimate their age within one or two years.

Some websites and social media companies such as Meta have argued that age verification should be done by app store owners, such as Apple and Google, and not individual platforms. This would mean that app stores would have to verify their users’ ages before they allow them to download apps. Unsurprisingly, Apple and Google disagree.

“Billed as ‘simple’ by its backers, including Meta, this proposal fails to cover desktop computers or other devices that are commonly shared within families. It also could be ineffective against pre-installed apps,” Google said in a blog post last year.

Privacy concerns remain an obstacle

Age checks are meant to keep kids out of online spaces that are not safe or appropriate for them, whether that’s social media or adult websites. But critics of online age verification see a worrisome trend toward a less secure, less private and less free internet, where people can be denied access not just to pornography but news, health information and the ability to speak openly and anonymously.

What’s considered harmful to minors can be subjective, and this is where experts believe laws requiring age verification can run afoul of the First Amendment. The question could lead to people being required to verify their ages to access anything, from Netflix to a neighborhood blog.

The digital rights group Electronic Frontier Foundation has been warning for years about “age-gating the internet.”

“(No) matter the method, every system demands users hand over sensitive and immutable personal information that links their offline identity to their online activity,” EFF writes in a blog post. “Once that valuable data is collected, it can easily be leaked, hacked, or misused.”

—Barbara Ortutay, AP technology writer
items.summary: Of the child safety measures agreed to in Meta’s landmark legal settlement , no category contains more detailed requirements than its commitments on age assurance —and for good reason. No matter how well the protections work, they are of little use if Meta can’t tell which users are kids.

items.title: [ArchDaily] City Governments Transform Industrial Buildings into Circular Construction Hubs in New York, London, and Brussels
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

During the last week of August, the New York City government announced a new project for the MADE Bush Terminal in Sunset Park, Brooklyn. It involves the transformation of the old industrial building into a center for the recovery, storage, sorting, and redistribution of construction materials during a one-year pilot program. The initiative echoes a wave of similar circular construction hubs recently launched or announced across Europe: a converted warehouse in Brussels, an industrial site adaptation in East London's Royal Docks, and a cross-border network supported by CirCoFin spanning Munich, Copenhagen, Lisbon, and Scotland, each repurposing industrial buildings and infrastructure to support the reuse of construction materials.
